text: What is the time complexity of searching for a value in a balanced binary search tree with n nodes?
hint: Each comparison lets you discard one subtree. Think about how many times n can be halved.
explanation: A balanced BST has height about log2(n), and each step moves one level down, so search takes O(log n).

text: Which data structure processes elements in first-in, first-out (FIFO) order?
hint: Picture people waiting in line at a ticket counter.
explanation: A queue removes elements in the order they were added: first in, first out.

text: Which data structure does a programming language runtime use to keep track of active function calls?
hint: The most recently called function is always the first one to return.
explanation: Function calls follow last-in, first-out order, which is exactly how the call stack works.

text: What is the average-case time to look up a key in a hash table with a good hash function and a low load factor?
hint: A good hash function jumps straight to a bucket that holds only a few items.
explanation: With uniform hashing and a bounded load factor, each bucket holds a constant number of keys on average, so lookup is O(1).

text: Two different keys produce the same hash index. What is this called?
hint: Two keys are trying to occupy the same slot.
explanation: A collision happens when distinct keys map to the same index. Chaining and open addressing are ways to resolve it.

text: Which sorting algorithm has a worst-case time complexity of O(n log n) and is stable?
hint: Consider both requirements: a guaranteed worst case, and keeping equal elements in their original order.
explanation: Merge sort always splits in half and merges in linear time, giving O(n log n) in every case, and a careful merge keeps equal elements in order.

text: What is the worst-case time complexity of quick sort when the pivot is always the smallest element?
hint: If the pivot is the smallest element, how big is each partition?
explanation: With the smallest element as the pivot, each partition removes only one element, giving n + (n-1) + ... + 1 = O(n^2) comparisons.

text: In a singly linked list, which operation takes O(1) time if you only have a pointer to the head?
hint: Which operation does not require walking through the list?
explanation: Inserting at the beginning only requires pointing the new node at the current head and updating the head pointer.

text: Which traversal of a binary search tree visits the keys in ascending order?
hint: In a BST, every key in the left subtree is smaller than the node and every key in the right subtree is larger.
explanation: In-order traversal visits left subtree, node, right subtree, which outputs BST keys in sorted order.

text: In a binary min-heap, where is the smallest element always stored?
hint: Recall the heap property between a parent and its children.
explanation: Every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the minimum must be at the root.

text: Which algorithm finds the shortest path from one source in a graph with non-negative edge weights?
hint: The algorithm repeatedly picks the unvisited vertex with the smallest known distance.
explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm greedily settles the closest unvisited vertex, which is correct when edge weights are non-negative.

text: Breadth-first search on an unweighted graph is typically implemented with which data structure?
hint: BFS explores all neighbours at the current distance before moving further out.
explanation: A queue makes BFS process vertices in order of discovery, level by level.

text: An algorithm runs two nested loops, each from 1 to n, with constant work inside. What is its time complexity?
hint: Count how many times the inner body runs for each pass of the outer loop.
explanation: The inner body runs n times for each of the n outer iterations, giving n × n = O(n^2).

text: What is the time complexity of accessing the element at index i in an array?
hint: Arrays store elements in one contiguous block of memory.
explanation: The address is base + i × element size, computed directly, so access is O(1).

text: Dynamic programming is most useful for problems that have overlapping subproblems and which other property?
hint: Think about how the best solution to the whole problem relates to the best solutions of its parts.
explanation: Dynamic programming needs optimal substructure (optimal solutions are built from optimal sub-solutions) plus overlapping subproblems to reuse.
